cards.meaning: Talking a lot, especially in a way that gives more details than other people need.
cards.nuance: Often mildly critical: it suggests someone is noisy, eager to share information, or unable to keep a secret.

uses.sentence: Our garrulous client explained every possible change, so I asked him to focus on the three we could make this week.
uses.tip: Use it when talking about someone who talks too much, not simply someone who is friendly.

uses.sentence: After drinks, my garrulous cousin had told everyone the story twice.
uses.tip: The word often has a humorous tone among friends or family.

uses.sentence: She is a strong analyst, though her garrulous style sometimes makes meetings longer than necessary.
uses.tip: A useful formal alternative to simply saying someone talks too much.

origin.summary: From the Latin garrulus, meaning talkative or chattering. The word was borrowed into English with the sense of being excessively talkative.

timeline.text: Garrulus means talkative, noisy or prone to chatter.
The word enters English as garrulous.
It describes people who talk freely and at great length.

cards.pitfall: It is stronger and more critical than chatty, which can simply describe someone who enjoys conversation.

cards.meaning: Willing to give or share more than you need, especially with time, money or help.
cards.nuance: It often suggests a generous attitude rather than simply having plenty. It can also mean giving someone more space, credit or opportunity than they expected.

uses.sentence: Mina was generous with her praise, giving the whole team credit for the successful launch.
uses.tip: Use it to describe giving more time, credit or support than others might expect.

uses.sentence: He was generous and bought us dinner as well as tickets to the show.
uses.tip: This is a natural way to describe someone who treats others to something special.

uses.sentence: Thank you for being so generous with your time and advice; your help made a real difference.
uses.tip: It works well in formal thanks when you want to praise someone’s willingness to give.

origin.summary: From the Latin generosus, originally meaning ‘of a noble kind’ and later developing the sense of ‘giving freely or abundantly’.

timeline.text: Generosus meant ‘of a noble kind’, with an association with generous birth.
The word entered English and began to mean ‘open-handed’ or ‘giving freely’.
It describes giving generously of money, time, help, credit or space.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use generous when you mean merely generous in quantity; for example, a ‘generous portion’ can simply mean a large one.

cards.meaning: Warm, cheerful and pleasant to be around.
cards.nuance: It suggests an easygoing, approachable person or atmosphere. It is warmer and slightly more formal than simply saying someone is nice.

uses.where: Team meeting · welcoming a new colleague
uses.sentence: Our genial sales manager always makes new clients feel comfortable.
uses.tip: Use it for someone whose relaxed manner puts others at ease.

uses.sentence: We had a relaxed meal with our genial host, who kept introducing us to interesting people.
uses.tip: It works well when you want to praise someone’s naturally sociable manner.

uses.sentence: The hotel had a genial atmosphere, with friendly staff and a welcoming common room.
uses.tip: It can describe a place as comfortably and sociable as it describes a person.

origin.summary: From Latin genialis, connected with weddings and festive occasions and ultimately with genius, an ancient idea of a protective spirit. English later developed the sense of being warm and pleasant.

timeline.text: Latin genialis referred to weddings, festivals and their protective spirits.
The word entered English with meanings connected with marriage and celebration.
It began to describe people as friendly, cheerful and pleasant to meet.

cards.pitfall: In older British English, genial could also mean suitable for a particular age group; avoid that dated sense in modern use.

cards.meaning: Strangely ugly, shocking, or unreal in a way that makes people feel disturbed or confused.
cards.nuance: The word describes something unnatural or unsettling, often exaggerated to an extreme degree. It can also mean simply bizarre, but usually carries a stronger sense of shock or discomfort.

uses.sentence: The cartoon’s exaggerated proportions made the mascot feel grotesque rather than friendly.
uses.tip: Use it for something deliberately distorted and unsettling, not merely unattractive.

uses.where: At a party · reacting to a costume
uses.sentence: His rubber mask was so grotesque that nobody could tell whether he was joking.
uses.tip: This use suggests exaggerated features or behaviour that make someone uneasy.

uses.sentence: The play turns a political scandal into a grotesque comedy, making every serious character look absurd.
uses.tip: In criticism, it often describes a deliberately exaggerated, disturbing style.

origin.summary: It came through French from Italian grottesco, meaning ‘of a grotto’, because the style was associated with strange murals found in underground Roman chambers.

timeline.text: Grotesque wall paintings appear in underground rooms, mixing human, animal and plant forms.
Italian artists copy these designs, and grottesco becomes an artistic term for their strange, decorative style.
The word reaches French and then English, initially referring to a style of ornament.
It mainly means bizarre, shockingly ugly or unsettling.

cards.pitfall: It can describe a person’s appearance or behaviour, so avoid using it as a casual substitute for ‘ugly’.

cards.meaning: Unlucky or unlucky in a way that seems especially undeserved.
cards.nuance: It often suggests that someone has been caught in an unfortunate situation through bad luck or poor judgement. The tone can be sympathetic, amused or gently critical.

uses.sentence: The hapless designer lost the only copy of the file just before the client call.
uses.tip: Use it for an unlucky mistake or mishap, especially when the result is clearly bad luck.

uses.where: At a party · spilling a drink
uses.sentence: My hapless friend knocked over her glass before anyone had even taken their coat off.
uses.tip: It sounds lightly teasing when describing someone’s repeated social blunders.

uses.sentence: After a hapless journey involving three wrong train platforms, we finally reached the venue.
uses.tip: A slightly literary or humorous option that adds colour to an account of mishaps.

origin.summary: Built from hap, meaning chance or luck, and the suffix -less, so the word originally suggested being without good fortune.

timeline.text: Hap traces to a word meaning chance, luck or fortune.
The noun hap is used for luck, good or bad, and for an occasion or chance event.
Hapless emerges in English, combining hap with the suffix -less.
It means unlucky or unfortunate, often with a sense of comic misfortune.

cards.pitfall: Hapless means unlucky or subject to misfortune; it does not mean unable to act, as helpless does.

cards.meaning: Behaviouring as if you are more important or superior than other people.
cards.nuance: It describes an exaggerated sense of status or self-importance, often shown by looking down on others. It can be mocking or disapproval, rather than simply describing someone as proud.

uses.sentence: Her haughty response to the suggestion made the rest of us reluctant to speak up.
uses.tip: Use it for behaviour that clearly shows superiority or disdain.

uses.sentence: He was too haughty to acknowledge the guests who had travelled a long way.
uses.tip: It often implies that someone is treating others as though they are beneath them.

uses.sentence: The haughty aristocrat refused to speak to the servants, even when her mother called his name.
uses.tip: A strong word for characterisation, especially when showing class or social distance.

origin.summary: It comes from French haut, meaning “high”, with an ending that was added when the word entered English.

timeline.text: The root haut meant “high” and came from the Latin word altus.
Haut developed into a form used to mean lofty or proud in appearance.
The word enters English in the sense of proud or arrogant.
It is mainly used to describe someone who acts superior to others.

cards.pitfall: Haughty suggests visible superiority or disdain; arrogant focuses more broadly on excessive pride or self-importance.

cards.meaning: Exaggerated theatrical behaviour used to attract attention or provoke a reaction.
cards.nuance: The word is usually critical, suggesting that someone is behaving dramatically rather than responding sincerely. It often implies a performance calculated to influence others.

uses.sentence: She dismissed the suggestion with such histrionics that nobody could tell whether she was genuinely upset.
uses.tip: Use it for conspicuously dramatic behaviour, especially when the reaction seems designed to command attention.

uses.sentence: His histrionics turned an ordinary disagreement into a scene everyone remembered.
uses.tip: This often sounds sharp or dismissive, so avoid it when describing ordinary enthusiasm.

uses.sentence: The report avoids personal attacks and focuses on the histrionics that made the meeting unproductive.
uses.tip: A formal alternative is dramatic behaviour; choose the stronger word when the behaviour is clearly excessive.

origin.summary: From Latin histrio, meaning actor or performer, ultimately connected with a Greek word for an actor. The English form developed in the context of acting and theatrical display.

timeline.text: Greek and Latin words for actors and performers form the root of the word.
Histrionics enters English with associations of acting and theatrical performance.
It chiefly means exaggerated behaviour displayed for effect.

cards.pitfall: Use it for deliberate or excessive performance, not for an ordinary emotional reaction. In medicine, histrionic personality traits can also refer to attention-seeking behaviour.

cards.meaning: Not thinking highly of yourself and willing to learn, improve, or accept that others may have a better idea.
cards.nuance: It can suggest genuine modesty and openness, but it can also sound overly self-effacing or excessively deferential.

uses.where: Team discussion · offering a different view
uses.sentence: I have a humble suggestion: what if we test this with customers before we build the full feature?
uses.tip: Use it to introduce an idea without sounding defensive or self-important.

uses.where: Dinner with friends · receiving a compliment
uses.sentence: Thank you — I’m just happy to help, and I’m still humble about my cooking.
uses.tip: This sounds light and friendly when you are sincerely pleased by the praise.

uses.where: Email to a mentor · asking for feedback
uses.sentence: I’d be humble to hear where you think I could improve before the presentation next week.
uses.tip: It softens a request for advice and shows that you are open to criticism.

origin.summary: Humble comes through Old French from Latin humilis, meaning low or humble. Its roots connect it with the earth, suggesting something modest or low.

timeline.text: Humilis means ‘low’ or ‘humble’ and is associated with humus, the earth.
The word appears as humble, carrying the sense of low-standing or modest.
It enters English and gradually develops its modern meanings of modest and unassuming.
It commonly describes a person’s attitude, manner, or willingness to learn.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use humble when you mean merely quiet or low-status; it focuses mainly on modesty and an absence of pride.

cards.meaning: The quality of being modest about your own abilities, achievements or importance.
cards.nuance: Humility is often shown by listening, giving others credit and being willing to learn. It does not mean thinking you are worthless or letting others walk over you.

uses.where: Team presentation · reviewing a successful launch
uses.sentence: She accepted the praise graciously, but gave most of the credit to the team.
uses.tip: Humility often appears through what you do, not just through the word itself.

uses.sentence: He showed real humility by asking about everyone else instead of talking about his promotion.
uses.tip: Use it when you want to describe someone who avoids making a big show of their success.

uses.sentence: The experience taught her that effective leadership required patience, humility and a willingness to admit mistakes.
uses.tip: It fits naturally in thoughtful writing about leadership, learning and personal growth.

origin.summary: Humility comes from Latin humilitas, meaning lowliness or a low position, and originally carried a religious sense of being humble before God.

timeline.text: Humilitas develops from humus, meaning earth or ground.
The word enters English through Old French and Latin religious writing.
It describes modesty, openness to learning and lack of excessive pride.

cards.pitfall: Humility is not the same as submissiveness; you can be modest without surrendering your opinions or boundaries.

cards.meaning: Someone who challenges accepted beliefs, customs, or influential figures.
cards.nuance: The word suggests more than ordinary disagreement: an iconoclast attacks ideas or symbols that others treat as beyond question. It can be complimentary or critical, depending on the context.

uses.where: Product review · questioning an established process
uses.sentence: Our newest engineer is an iconoclast who keeps asking why we still use this approval process.
uses.tip: Use it for someone who challenges company routines or accepted ways of working.

uses.where: Gallery opening · discussing an unusual exhibition
uses.sentence: Her work is that of an iconoclast, turning familiar objects into strange new questions.
uses.tip: It works well for describing artists, rebels, and outspoken thinkers.

uses.where: Culture article · introducing a controversial figure
uses.sentence: Rather than a conventional rebel, he was an iconoclast who questioned the institutions his supporters admired.
uses.tip: Pair it with a clear target of the person’s criticism to avoid sounding vague.

origin.summary: Built from Greek roots meaning ‘image’ and ‘breaker’. It originally referred to someone who destroyed religious images and later broadened to describe challengers of established beliefs.

timeline.text: The roots combine eikon, meaning ‘image’, with klastos, meaning ‘broken’.
The word becomes associated with people who attacked or destroyed religious images.
Its meaning expands to include people who oppose accepted beliefs, institutions, or conventions.
It usually describes a person who challenges powerful or widely accepted ideas.

cards.pitfall: An iconoclast challenges established ideas or symbols; an icon is the image, object, or person being treated as important.

cards.meaning: Calm and controlled, especially when a difficult or unexpected situation might cause other people to react strongly.
cards.nuance: It suggests steady self-control rather than a lack of concern. It can sound slightly formal or even admiringly detached.

uses.sentence: She remained imperturbable when the client challenged the proposal.
uses.tip: Use it to emphasize composure under pressure.

uses.sentence: Uncle Miguel was imperturbable despite the argument around the table.
uses.tip: It often describes someone who does not visibly react to conflict.

uses.sentence: Her imperturbable handling of a last-minute technical failure impressed the leadership team.
uses.tip: It sounds polished in reports and formal evaluations.

origin.summary: From Latin imperturbabilis, meaning ‘not able to be disturbed’, built on perturbare, ‘to disturb’.

timeline.text: Imperturbabilis means ‘not perturbable’ or ‘not to be disturbed’.
The word enters English with the sense of being unmoved or uncontrollable.
It is mainly used in formal English for calmness under pressure.

cards.pitfall: Use it for deliberate self-control; for simple relaxation, ‘calm’ is usually more natural.

cards.meaning: Acting quickly and without enough thought, often because of strong feelings or enthusiasm.
cards.nuance: It can suggest sudden, forceful action that may lead to mistakes. It is also used for people who are energetic, impulsive and eager to act.

uses.sentence: His impetuous decision to release the feature early created problems for the support team.
uses.tip: Use it to describe a rash decision made with little planning.

uses.sentence: We became impetuous and took the coastal route without checking the weather.
uses.tip: It fits spontaneous actions driven by excitement or impatience.

uses.where: Incident report · describing a sudden move
uses.sentence: The manager describes the change as impetuous rather than a considered response to the risks.
uses.tip: This sounds analytical and slightly critical, so it suits formal reports.

origin.summary: From Latin impetus, meaning ‘force’ or ‘impulse’, through the French impétueux.

timeline.text: Impetus means ‘force, drive or impulse’.
The adjective enters English through French, describing forceful or impulsive action.
It mainly means acting quickly without careful thought.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it as a simple synonym for ‘energetic’; it usually carries the idea of acting without enough thought.

cards.meaning: Unable or unwilling to be softened, calmed, or changed.
cards.nuance: It describes a person, attitude, or hostility that persists despite attempts to ease the situation. It is strong and often suggests a stubborn refusal to make peace.

uses.sentence: Her opposition to the proposal remained implacable despite weeks of discussion.
uses.tip: Use it when someone’s position will not soften, even after repeated efforts to negotiate.

uses.sentence: His resentment was implacable, and he refused to speak to either of them.
uses.tip: It can describe deep personal resentment that cannot be easily calmed.

uses.sentence: The two governments remained implacable rivals throughout the decade.
uses.tip: A strong choice for formal writing about hostility or rivalry that will not soften.

origin.summary: From Latin implacabilis, meaning ‘unappeasable’, formed from in-, ‘not’, and placare, ‘to calm or appease’.

timeline.text: Implacabilis is formed from roots meaning ‘not’ and ‘to calm or appease’.
The word enters English with the sense of impossible to calm or soften.
It describes hostility, opposition, or resentment that cannot be appeased.

cards.pitfall: Implacable focuses on a person or attitude that cannot be calmed; inexorable more often describes a process or force that cannot be stopped.

cards.meaning: Happening without intention or careful thought.
cards.nuance: It describes an action, mistake or effect that was not planned. It often suggests the person involved did not mean to cause it.

uses.sentence: The missing figures were an inadvertent result of copying the wrong version of the spreadsheet.
uses.tip: Use it to describe an unintended mistake without assigning deliberate blame.

uses.sentence: My inadvertent comment about the food made everyone uncomfortable.
uses.tip: It works when you want to admit that something awkward was unintentional.

uses.sentence: Please accept my apologies for the inadvertent omission of your name in the previous message.
uses.tip: A formal way to acknowledge an error or something said without thinking.

origin.summary: Built from Latin words meaning ‘not attentive’, and later came to mean ‘unintentional’.

timeline.text: First used for something done without attention or thought.
The meaning shifted clearly toward ‘unintentional’ or ‘unplanned’.
Common in formal writing for an unintended action or effect.

cards.pitfall: Use inadvertent for something done without intention; it does not mean that nobody noticed it.

cards.meaning: Inclined to avoid effort, activity or action.
cards.nuance: Often suggests a settled habit of laziness rather than ordinary tiredness or a temporary lack of motivation. It has a literary or old-fashioned tone.

uses.sentence: His indolent attitude during slow periods is limiting his chances of promotion.
uses.tip: Use it in formal criticism when someone consistently shows little willingness to act.

uses.where: Weekend plans · waiting for a friend
uses.sentence: On lazy Sunday mornings, we are both too indolent to make plans before noon.
uses.tip: It can sound playful when describing a familiar habit between friends.

uses.sentence: The novel paints him as indolent and unwilling to confront the problems he has created.
uses.tip: Common in literary writing for portraying passivity or refusal to act.

origin.summary: From Latin indolens, meaning ‘unwilling to work’ or ‘idle’, built from in-, meaning ‘not’, and dolere, meaning ‘to suffer’.

timeline.text: Indolens forms from in-, ‘not’, and dolere, ‘to suffer’, describing someone who avoids pain or effort.
The word enters English in formal and literary contexts.
It remains mainly literary or deliberately formal, especially when describing habitual passivity.

cards.pitfall: Indolent usually describes a habit or character trait, so it can sound too severe for someone who is merely tired, busy or temporarily unmotivated.

cards.meaning: Existing as a natural and permanent part of something.
cards.nuance: It often suggests that a quality or problem cannot be removed without changing the basic nature of the thing. Use it for qualities, risks and limitations that are built into a situation or design.

uses.sentence: There is some inherent risk in combining customer data from separate systems.
uses.tip: Use it to describe a risk or limitation built into a process, product or decision.

uses.sentence: There’s an inherent trust between us that makes it easy to talk openly.
uses.tip: It sounds thoughtful when describing a quality that is central to a person or relationship.

uses.sentence: The delay is inherent in the approval process, so we have allowed extra time.
uses.tip: Pair it with words such as risk, feature, weakness or characteristic for a precise tone.

origin.summary: From Latin inhaerens, meaning ‘sticking to’ or ‘remaining attached to’, which developed into the idea of something being naturally connected to something else.

timeline.text: Inhaerere means ‘to stick to’ or ‘remain attached to’.
Inherent enters English in the sense of firmly connected or inseparable.
It is commonly used for qualities, risks and limitations that are built into something.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use inherent to mean simply important; it means the quality is naturally or structurally part of something.

cards.meaning: Present from birth or built into the basic nature of something.
cards.nuance: It describes qualities that seem natural or instinctive rather than developed through learning. It is often used for abilities, traits and patterns that are thought to be universal.

uses.where: Team discussion · assessing a new hire
uses.sentence: She has an innate ability to spot problems before they become serious.
uses.tip: Use it for a quality that seems to come naturally rather than from training.

uses.sentence: His curiosity seems innate; even as a child, he wanted to understand how things worked.
uses.tip: It sounds thoughtful when describing a natural personal quality.

uses.sentence: The study suggests that some forms of attention are innate, although experience can shape how they develop.
uses.tip: Use it carefully in arguments about what people are born with.

origin.summary: From Latin innatus, meaning 'born into' or 'natural', based on nasci, 'to be born'.

timeline.text: Innatus develops from innasci, 'to be born into', with the sense of something natural or inherent.
The word enters English in the sense of existing from birth.
It is used for natural qualities, abilities and patterns in people, animals or other things.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use innate simply to mean something you like or find natural; it usually suggests a quality present from the beginning.

cards.meaning: Brave and willing to face danger, difficulty or unfamiliar challenges.
cards.nuance: It suggests boldness with a sense of adventure, often used for people or actions that inspire admiration. It is more literary than everyday alternatives such as “brave” or “fearless.”

uses.where: Team briefing · entering a new market
uses.sentence: The intrepid team took the assignment despite the tight deadline and unfamiliar requirements.
uses.tip: Use it for people or teams whose boldness deserves admiration.

uses.sentence: intrepid explorers crossed the mountains before the weather turned.
uses.tip: It adds a grand, adventurous tone to stories about challenging journeys.

uses.sentence: She became an intrepid advocate for workers who had long been ignored.
uses.tip: A slightly elevated word that can make a tribute sound especially strong.

origin.summary: From Latin intrepidus, formed from in-, meaning ‘without’, and trepidus, meaning ‘trembling’ or ‘agitated’. The original sense was ‘undismayed’ or ‘untroubled by fear’.

timeline.text: Intrepidus develops from in- ‘without’ and trepidus ‘trembling’, giving the sense of being free from fear.
The word enters English through French and Latin usage.
It means brave, daring and ready to face challenges.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it as a synonym for reckless; intrepid describes courage, while reckless suggests acting without enough thought.

cards.meaning: Strongly established or firmly fixed, especially as a habit, tendency, or long-lasting problem.
cards.nuance: It often suggests something that has continued for a long time and is difficult to change. It can describe personal habits and preferences, but it is especially negative when describing conflict, prejudice, or problems.

uses.where: Team meeting · addressing a recurring delay
uses.sentence: Late submissions are an inveterate problem, so we need a clearer deadline and a named owner.
uses.tip: Use it for a problem that keeps returning despite previous attempts to fix it.

uses.sentence: My inveterate habit of saying yes has left me with no free evenings this month.
uses.tip: It adds emphasis to a long-standing personal habit, sometimes with a mildly self-critical tone.

uses.sentence: The article examines the inveterate distrust that some communities have toward institutions.
uses.tip: It is well suited to formal discussion of entrenched attitudes, disputes, or problems.

origin.summary: From Latin inveteratus, meaning ‘aged’ or ‘long established’, based on inveterescere, ‘to grow old’.

timeline.text: Inveteratus means ‘aged’ and comes from vetus, ‘old’, with the prefix in-, suggesting becoming or being made old.
Entered English in the sense of old, experienced, or firmly established.
Usually describes a habit, tendency, or problem that is deeply established and persistent.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it for something that is simply old; it normally implies that the thing is firmly established or difficult to change.

cards.meaning: Cheerful, lively, and self-confident, often with a slightly showy or swaggering manner.
cards.nuance: It suggests someone is enjoying themselves and carrying themselves with bold confidence. The word can sound admiring, but it may also imply that someone is being a little too pleased with themselves.

uses.where: Team stand-up · matching the new campaign
uses.sentence: Her jaunty presentation gave a plain product update some extra energy.
uses.tip: Best for creative or informal settings; it can sound too playful in a serious update.

uses.sentence: He arrived in a jaunty suit, already ready to tell everyone the story of the day.
uses.tip: Use it for an appearance or manner that feels cheerful and slightly showy.

uses.sentence: She walked into the quiet room with a jaunty grin and an air of triumph.
uses.tip: It adds personality to a description without directly stating the character’s confidence.

origin.summary: Probably borrowed from French jante, an old word connected with neatness or graceful bearing, though the exact route is uncertain.

timeline.text: The word first appears in English with meanings connected with neatness, fashion, or a graceful manner.
Its meaning develops toward cheerful confidence and a dashing, swaggering style.
It describes a lively, self-assured manner that may be slightly exaggerated.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use jaunty simply to mean cheerful; it usually includes noticeable confidence, style, or swagger.

cards.meaning: Not strict or careful enough about rules, standards or responsibilities.
cards.nuance: It can describe relaxed people, loose controls or poor attention to detail. It often suggests that something needs to be tightened rather than that the situation is impossible.

uses.sentence: Our deadline checks have been lax, so we need a clearer process from this week.
uses.tip: Use it for rules, supervision, discipline or attention to detail.

uses.where: Dinner with friends · choosing a restaurant
uses.sentence: Let’s be a bit lax tonight and order whatever looks best.
uses.tip: In relaxed social contexts, it can mean pleasantly easygoing.

uses.sentence: The department was lax in its tracking of client complaints.
uses.tip: This sounds formal and critical; explain what was not done properly.

origin.summary: From Latin laxus, meaning loose, slack or not tightly held. English later extended the idea to rules and standards that are not enforced firmly enough.

timeline.text: laxus, ‘loose, slack, relaxed’.
The word enters English and is used for physical looseness.
It develops meanings connected with weak discipline and insufficiently strict standards.

cards.pitfall: Lax usually means insufficiently strict, not simply relaxed or comfortable.

cards.meaning: Lenient means not strict about rules, mistakes or required standards.
cards.nuance: It can describe a fair, understanding approach, but it may also suggest that someone is letting standards slip.

uses.sentence: Our manager was lenient about the missed deadline because the team was dealing with an urgent client issue.
uses.tip: Use it when explaining why a rule or penalty was applied gently.

uses.where: Hosting dinner · a friend arrives late
uses.sentence: Be lenient with Sam tonight; he was delayed by the traffic and looked exhausted.
uses.tip: It often sounds kind and understanding in informal conversations.

uses.sentence: The examiner took a lenient approach, allowing minor formatting errors without reducing the overall grade.
uses.tip: A useful alternative to ‘not strict’ when you want a more formal tone.

origin.summary: From Latin lenientia, meaning ‘tolerance’ or mildness, related to lenire, ‘to soften or make less harsh’.

timeline.text: Lenire means ‘to soften or make less harsh’, while lenientia refers to mildness or tolerance.
The word enters English with meanings connected with mild treatment and reduced strictness.
It describes people, rules or approaches that are gentle rather than strict.

cards.pitfall: In a legal context, ‘lenient’ usually means less strict in imposing punishment, not more tolerant in general.

cards.meaning: Generous and forgiving, especially when you could respond negatively to someone or treat them harshly.
cards.nuance: It suggests a big-hearted reaction that rises above a personal conflict. It sounds respectful but can be slightly formal or old-fashioned in everyday conversation.

uses.sentence: She was magnanimous after the mistake, focusing on what the team could improve together.
uses.tip: Use it when describing a generous, gracious response to a setback.

uses.where: Family gathering · overlooking an awkward remark
uses.sentence: He was magnanimous about the misunderstanding and carried on as though it had never happened.
uses.tip: It fits a generous reaction that avoids holding on to anger or resentment.

uses.sentence: The judges were magnanimous in recognising both finalists for their excellent work.
uses.tip: Use it in formal writing to praise fairness, generosity or a gracious attitude.

origin.summary: From Latin magnanimus, meaning ‘great-souled’: magnus means ‘great’, and animus means ‘spirit’ or ‘soul’.

timeline.text: Magnanimus combines magnus, ‘great’, with animus, ‘spirit’ or ‘soul’.
The word enters English, initially carrying the sense of being noble or great-hearted.
It mainly describes generosity, fairness and a willingness to overlook conflict.

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with magnificent, which means impressive or splendid in appearance or achievement.

cards.meaning: Unable to adapt one's behaviour, emotions, or social expectations well enough to cope with everyday demands.
cards.nuance: Often used in psychological or older formal contexts, but it can sound blunt or insulting when applied directly to someone.

uses.where: Employee support · helping a new hire
uses.sentence: Because the new hire seemed maladjusted to the office routine, her manager offered mentoring rather than criticism.
uses.tip: Use this in a formal or clinical context, not as a quick judgement about a colleague.

uses.sentence: Some older relatives use maladjusted for anyone who ignores family customs.
uses.tip: The word may sound old-fashioned or judgemental in casual conversation.

uses.where: Clinical assessment · describing a client's needs
uses.sentence: In the assessment, maladjusted was too broad, so the author described the client's social anxiety more precisely.
uses.tip: It fits formal reports, but a specific description is usually clearer and more respectful.

origin.summary: Built from the English prefix mal-, meaning 'badly' or 'wrongly', and adjusted, meaning 'adapted'.

timeline.text: The prefix mal- was established in English for 'badly' or 'wrongly'.
Maladjusted becomes established as a description of poor personal or social adjustment.
Its use is mainly clinical, formal, or dated, and it is often considered harsh.

cards.pitfall: Avoid using it as a casual insult; name the specific difficulty or behaviour instead.

cards.meaning: Easy to shape, bend or influence without breaking.
cards.nuance: For materials, it describes flexibility. For people or plans, it suggests someone or something can be strongly influenced, which may be intended or viewed as a weakness.

uses.sentence: The early plan is malleable, so we can adjust it after the client clarifies their priorities.
uses.tip: Use it when a proposal or strategy can still be changed easily.

uses.sentence: She’s more malleable than she was, and she now considers views different from her own.
uses.tip: This can sound mildly critical, suggesting excessive willingness to change.

uses.sentence: The alloy is highly malleable, allowing it to be shaped into thin, precise panels.
uses.tip: For physical materials, it is more precise than simply flexible.

origin.summary: From Latin malleare, meaning ‘to hammer or beat into shape’, related to malleus, ‘hammer’.

timeline.text: Malleare means ‘to hammer or shape by beating’, from malleus, ‘hammer’.
Enters English describing metal that can be hammered into shape.
The meaning broadens to describe anything easily shaped or influenced.

cards.pitfall: When describing people, malleable can imply that someone is easily influenced or too compliant.
